title: The Dormition
hookLine: the Orthodox call the August feast of Mary her falling asleep
tomorrow: Mary close: do whatever he tells you

lines: MARY ON A LOW BED, APOSTLES GRIEVING.
CHRIST HOLDS A SMALL SWADDLED FIGURE.
cards: Look closely at the icon. Mary lies on a low bed, eyes closed, hands folded. Around her stand the apostles, bent with grief.

One leans down close to her face; others hold their hands to their cheeks. Behind the bed, taller than everyone, stands Christ, in light. In his arms he holds a small figure wrapped in white, like a newborn.
That small figure is Mary's soul. Think of the Christmas icons: a mother holding her swaddled child. Here it's turned around.
The son holds his mother, swaddled, and carries her home. Orthodox Christians have a name for this feast, and it isn't death.

teach.b: You met the Assumption back in year one. First, the name. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Koimesis, the falling asleep; in Latin, Dormition.
It's the feast the Latin Church calls the Assumption, and Eastern Catholics keep it as the Dormition too. Second, why sleep. The New Testament uses that word for the death of the faithful.

teach.h: HE FELL ASLEEP IN THE LORD.
teach.b: When Stephen is stoned, the Douay-Rheims says that, having prayed for the men killing him, "he fell asleep in the Lord."
Paul writes to the Thessalonians about those who are asleep, so they won't grieve like people without hope. You only call it sleep if you expect a waking. Third, the story.
The Bible doesn't tell how Mary's life ended. Tradition says the apostles were gathered to her bedside, that she was laid in a tomb, and that her body was not left there.
The icon comes from that tradition, not from a Gospel, and the Church keeps the two apart.
Fourth, two names for one hope.
The Catholic Church teaches, as dogma, that Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.
Notice the phrasing: Pius the Twelfth defined the Assumption without deciding whether she died first. The Catechism quotes an Eastern hymn about her falling asleep.
The Orthodox speak plainly of her death, and of her son taking her to himself. One tradition names the arrival, the other the moment of closing her eyes. Both point at the same door.

how: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians keep the feast of the Dormition with the Divine Liturgy and a fast beforehand; in the West, Catholics keep the same day as the Assumption, which in some countries is a holy day of obligation.

games.q: you're painting the icon of Mary's falling asleep. Christ stands behind her bed. what do you put in his arms?
o: a small figure wrapped in white, like a newborn.
games.why: he holds her soul, swaddled like a baby. in the Christmas icons she holds him; here the son carries his mother.

practice: Bring to mind an Orthodox church you've passed, an Orthodox Christian you know, or simply the candles lit before icons tonight, and hold them a few breaths with good will.
If you pray, use a short Byzantine refrain on the out-breath, most holy Mother of God, save us. If you don't, simply hold the picture: a son carrying his mother, gently, the way she once carried him.

wordCard.voice: Dormition. The falling asleep: the Eastern name for the end of Mary's earthly life, the feast the West calls the Assumption. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the falling asleep of the Theotokos, the Mother of God.

carryVoice: Your line: fell asleep. The Bible's old word for death, said with hope. Until tomorrow.
